variables.name: gdp
variables.label: GDP (nominal, local currency)
variables.units: nominal local currency; unit per country (millions AUD, millions BEF, billions CAD, billions DKK, millions FIM (new markka), billions FRF (new francs), billions DM, millions IEP) | nominal, national currency in the chapter unit (billions ITL/GBP/USD; trillions JPY; millions NLG/NOK/PTE/ESP/SEK/CHF)
variables.definition: Nominal gross domestic product in local currency (legacy currency for euro members, converted at the fixed conversion rate). | Nominal gross domestic product at current market prices in local currency.
variables.construction: Historical national accounts (MeasuringWorth for Australia; GGDC HNA for Belgium; Dincecco-Prado for Canada; Mitchell IHS for Denmark and France; Hjerppe for Finland; growth rates from Burhop-Wolff NNP, Ritschl-Spoerer GNP and Sensch for Germany; Gerlach-Stuart and CSO for Ireland) spliced with IMF IFS nominal GDP for the post-war period; wartime gaps filled from Bordo, Eichengreen, Klingebiel & Martinez-Peria (2001). | Historical national-accounts reconstructions (Baffigi; Ohkawa et al.; van Zanden/Smits; Grytten; Valerio; Prados de la Escosura; GGDC; Historical Statistics of Switzerland; Hills-Thomas-Dimsdale; Johnston-Williamson) spliced ('Level' or 'Chainlinked') onto IMF IFS / ONS / BEA / OECD nominal GDP for recent decades; euro-area countries converted back to legacy currency at the fixed conversion rate.

The text lists both "1953–2014 IFS" and "1980–2020 NBB" entries (overlapping 1980–2014) with the NBB 1953–1979 entry marked "Formerly"; the document does not say which source wins in the overlap. | Canada: The 1946–1947 citation (van Meerten, Capital formation in Belgium) appears to be a copy-paste error in the document for a Canadian series; starts 1871. | France: The 1920–1924 van Meerten (Belgium) citation for a French series appears to be a copy-paste error in the document; 1919 and 1945 missing. | Germany: Pre-1960 ratio is capital formation over NNP, not GDP; gaps 1914–1919, 1940–1947. The repeated van Meerten (Belgium) citations for German interwar years look like a copy-paste error in the document. | Ireland: Starts 1944; no source listed for 1970–1994 as printed. | JPN: Starts 1885; gap in 1945. | NLD: Gaps 1914-1920 and 1940-1947. variables.caveats: Early post-war values are black-market rates (Belgium 1946-53, Canada 1947-50, Denmark 1946-56, Finland 1946-60, France 1946-58). The Finland note misprints 'Belgian franc-euro' for the markka rate 5.94573. Germany 1945 missing. Per-country notes (pp. 21-100): Belgium: "We assume a Belgian franc-euro exchange rate of 40.3399 where necessary." 1946–1953 values are black-market rates. | Finland: "We assume a Belgian franc-euro exchange rate of 5.94573 where necessary." (sic — 5.94573 is the Finnish markka–euro conversion rate; the word "Belgian" is a copy-paste error in the document.) | France: "We assume a French franc-euro exchange rate of 6.55957 where necessary." | Germany: "We assume a German mark-euro exchange rate of 1.95583 where necessary." 1945 missing. | IRL: Punt pegged to sterling before 1979, so 1920-1978 derived from UK exchange-rate series. Punt-euro rate 0.787564 assumed where necessary. | ITA: Lira-euro rate 1936.27 assumed where necessary. | JPN: Gap 1871 and 1872. | NLD: Guilder-euro rate 2.20371 assumed where necessary. | PRT: Escudo-euro rate 200.482 assumed where necessary (text reads 'Italian Portugese escudo-euro'). | ESP: Peseta-euro rate 166.386 assumed where necessary (text reads 'Italian Spanish peseta-euro').

variables.caveats: Institutional coverage changes across splices; wartime gaps in most countries (Belgium 1914-19 and 1941-49; France 1939-45; Germany 1941-45). France 1980-2013 year-average of monthly values vs end-of-period elsewhere. Per-country notes (pp. 21-100): Australia: Gap 1946–1947 as printed. | Belgium: Starts 1885; gaps 1914–1919 and 1941–1949. Early segments are growth-rate splices from narrow institutional coverage (credit unions, bank current-account debtors); 1961–1979 covers a broad set of financial intermediaries (monetary institutions, savings banks, mortgage and capitalisation companies, life/accident insurers, pension funds). | Finland: "Bank of Finland (2012), ibid." refers to the series sent by email by Essi Tamminen (see Narrow/Broad Money). | France: Starts 1900; gap 1939–1945. 1958–1962 = credits financed by monetary resources + credits financed by public funds or other resources; 1963–1979 = bank credits in metropolitan France (banks + Banque de France); 1980–2013 year averages of monthly values vs end-of-period from 2014. | Germany: Gap 1941–1945; 1883–1940 includes interbank exposures; territorial changes (Reich → West Germany → unified Germany). | IRL: 2003-2020: only lending to households and non-financial corporations; lending to insurance corporations, pension funds and other financial intermediaries excluded. | JPN: Starts 1874; gap 1941-1945; 1992 interpolated as simple average of 1991 and 1993. | NLD: Starts 1900. | PRT: Gap 1904-1919 implied. | ESP: Starts 1900; gap 1936-1945. | SWE: Starts 1871. | GBR: Starts 1880. | USA: Starts 1880. Flow of Funds data include GSE and private mortgage backed securities held on balance sheet. 'Fraser Federal Reserve Archive (1959), ibid.' and 'United States Census Bureau, ibid.' are cited in full before p.101.

Jump in 2011 mortgages due to: "Over the course of 2011 data in this table were affected by conversion to International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS)" further: "Under the outgoing CGAAP, through the process of securitization and due to the subsequent sale of the corresponding debt or ABS, the originators of ABS do not report the securitized receivables and the corresponding securities on their own balance sheets. Under the incoming IFRS, these ABS and receivables will now be reported on the balance sheets of the companies themselves, as the originators of the ABS. This is an important change in financial reporting. As mentioned, currently the transfers of receivables off balance sheet are reported as sale transactions, but this will not be the case under IFRS. The consolidation on the originators' balance sheets will be the biggest change with respect to the Financial Flow Accounts and the National Balance Sheet Accounts. It is important to note that at the economy–wide level, neither lending via credit markets nor credit market debt will change; only the sectoral composition or distribution of the credit market assets and liabilities will be affected."

variables.caveats: Canada 2011 IFRS break handled by extending 1990-2010 with growth of an IFRS-unaffected aggregate. Germany 1927 linearly interpolated. Finland changes from loans secured by real estate to household housing loans in 1979. Belgium from 2003 covers individuals only. Per-country notes (pp. 21-100): Belgium: Gaps 1914–1919 and 1940–1949. From 2003 the series covers mortgage loans of individuals (households) only. | Canada: Starts 1874. Known break: 2011 IFRS conversion brought securitized mortgages back onto bank balance sheets; JST avoids the jump by extending 1990–2010 with growth rates of an IFRS-unaffected aggregate. | Denmark: Starts 1875. Danish "mortgage loans" = lending by mortgage-credit institutes (to households and non-financial corporations), not bank mortgages. | Finland: Starts 1927; gap 1932–1933. Concept changes from loans secured by real estate (all borrowers, 1934–1978) to housing loans to households (1979 on). | France: Gaps 1934–1945. Pre-1934 series track mortgage lending of the Crédit Foncier / Banque Hypothécaire only; 1946–1976 is housing credit ("crédits au logement"). | Germany: Starts 1883; gaps 1920–1923, 1941–1948; 1927 linearly interpolated; pre-1920 covers mortgage banks + Prussian savings banks only. | IRL: 2003-2020 figures exclude securitized loans and are best considered a measure of banking sector exposure rather than household exposure. | JPN: Starts 1893; gap 1941-1945. | NLD: Starts 1900; growth rates after 1986 from a spreadsheet shared by Tijmen Swank (DNB). | NOR: 1975-1977 calculated as previous year x 1.25. | PRT: Starts 1920. | ESP: Starts 1904; gap 1936-1945; 1985 = average of 1984 & 1986 (break in original series for unknown reason). | SWE: Starts 1871. | GBR: Starts 1880. | USA: Starts 1880.

variables.name: lev
variables.label: Banks, capital ratio (in %)
variables.definition: Capital ratio = Capital / Total Assets of the banking sector, in percent.
variables.construction: Computed from two documented components, Total Assets and Capital (see component entries). Where a source gives only a capital ratio (e.g. OECD Bank Profitability, APRA Tier 1 ratios, ECB tangible equity % of assets, Finnish interpolated 1990/91 ratios), the ratio is chainlinked and multiplied by the Total Assets series to obtain Capital.
variables.caveats: Coverage differs by country and period (Australia trading + savings banks; Belgium major credit institutions from 1920; Canada chartered banks; Denmark commercial + savings banks; Finland commercial banks/MFIs; France from 1890 via Mazbouri et al. then Commission de controle des banques, OECD, ECB; Germany Aktienbanken + Hypothekenbanken + Sparkassen then all banks). Capital definitions change (shareholder funds, Tier 1, tangible equity). Per-country notes (pp. 21-100): Australia: Built from two components, Total Assets and Capital, documented separately below. Where only a capital ratio is available from a source, the ratio is chainlinked and multiplied by the Total Assets series to compute Capital. | Belgium: Built from Total assets and Capital components below. | Canada: Built from Total Assets and Capital components below; chartered banks only. | Denmark: Built from Total Assets and Capital components below (commercial banks + savings banks). | Finland: Built from Total Assets and Capital components below; starts 1873. | France: Built from Total Assets and Capital components below; starts 1890. | Germany: Built from Total Assets and Capital components below. TERMS OF USE FOR THIS DATASET
This dataset was developed over many years with the generous financial support of the Institute for New Economic Thinking, the Volkswagen Foundation, and the German Federal Ministry of Education Research, and the European Research Council. We also thank our home institutions where we have conducted our research. Consistent with the terms of the support we have received from all of these organizations, our dataset is being made freely available in this noncommercial form.
We grant every user at no cost a license (see below) to use and/or share the licensed material, in whole or in part, provided that it is for non-commercial (e.g., academic) purposes, provided that our dataset is properly attributed and cited to credit the authors, and provided that it may only be shared under identical license terms. Commercial data providers are thus strictly forbidden to integrate all or parts of the dataset into their services and/or resell the data.
LICENCE TERMS
All users of this work agree to the terms of a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International License. The detailed terms of this license can be found here.
To comply with the attribution requirement in the license, whenever it is used the dataset must be cited as follows:
"Òscar Jordà, Moritz Schularick, and Alan M. Taylor. 2017. Macrofinancial History and the New Business Cycle Facts. in NBER Macroeconomics Annual 2016, volume 31, edited by Martin Eichenbaum and Jonathan A. Parker. Chicago: University of Chicago Press."
However, those using any data pertaining to asset prices or rates of return should cite Òscar Jordà, Katharina Knoll, Dmitry Kuvshinov, Moritz Schularick, and Alan M. Taylor. 2019. "The Rate of Return on Everything, 1870–2015." Quarterly Journal of Economics. Forthcoming.
We advise making explicit reference to the date when the database was consulted, as statistics are subject to revisions.
